composition: Binary Fe-Al alloy with a nominal Al content of 16 at.%, determined by ICP analysis to be 16.0 at.% Al (8.4 wt.-%); the balance is Fe of 99.99% purity purified by zone melting. Unavoidable impurities are deliberately kept low: 45 wt.ppm C, 40 wt.ppm Si, and 60 wt.ppm O. Al alloying is intended to provide solid-solution hardening, to reduce density and to give high oxidation and high-temperature corrosion resistance, while the low impurity level (C below 100 wt.ppm) was chosen to avoid confusing the intrinsic deformation behaviour with carbide precipitation, which is significant in Fe-Al alloys containing the more usual 300–600 wt.ppm C.
conclusions: For this specific sample the 14-day 320 °C anneal of the 45 ppm C Fe-16%Al monocrystal produced no carbides, showing that a low carbon content combined with the absence of grain boundaries suppresses carbide precipitation in this temperature/duration regime; carbide formation in the study required grain boundaries (polycrystals) or higher carbon plus concurrent loading (Fe-17%Al monocrystal). More broadly, the study concludes that short-range ordering in these low-impurity Fe-Al alloys has no major effect on deformation behaviour (only treatments above 600 °C matter significantly), that quenching produces excess vacancies which harden and which heal out only slowly, that the room-temperature yield stress rises linearly with Al up to 18 at.% via solid-solution hardening, that ductility falls correspondingly with a transition from ductile to brittle (necking-free) fracture between 15 and 18 at.% Al at room temperature and 12–14 at.% Al at −100 °C, that low-temperature yield-stress drops stem from mobile-dislocation/vacancy interactions, and that deformation twinning at low temperature arises from insufficient dislocation mobility. These findings matter for the development of low-density, high-strength Fe-Al sheet materials for structural/automotive use.

aliases: Fe-16%Al monocrystal with 45 ppm C after 14 days at 320 °C

mechanisms: Carbon availability and the absence of grain boundaries control carbide formation: the Fe-16%Al monocrystal contains only 45 wt.ppm C and has no grain boundaries, so the 14-day 320 °C anneal produced no detectable carbides, whereas polycrystals (which precipitate thin plate-like/rod-like carbides preferentially on grain boundaries) and the higher-carbon Fe-17%Al monocrystal (70 ppm C, carbides only under concurrent 100 MPa loading) do form carbides.

Heat treatments below 600 °C control the degree of short-range order (maximum ordering near 250 °C, minimum after quenching from 1100 or 600 °C), so the 320 °C/14 d treatment sets an intermediate state of short-range order; however, the hardness data do not reflect this pattern, so short-range ordering has no major impact on the hardness/deformation behaviour — only treatments above 600 °C affect the mechanical behaviour significantly.

Quenching from 1100 °C traps a high concentration of thermal excess vacancies (vacancy formation enthalpy only about 1–1.2 eV for Fe-16–18%Al), which are immobile at low temperature and act as obstacles to dislocation motion, producing the highest hardness; annealing below the quench temperature heals these vacancies out only slowly, so even 14 days at 300 °C may not fully eliminate them.

Solid-solution hardening of Al in bcc Fe gives a linear increase of yield stress with Al content (described by Suzuki's theory), so the Al-rich matrix of this crystal is inherently stronger than dilute Fe-Al; the corresponding decrease of fracture strain with increasing Al arises from reduced dislocation mobility, enhanced by quenched-in excess vacancies.

Reduced dislocation mobility in higher-Al and quenched Fe-Al crystals (evidenced by TEM: planar glide bands with straight dislocations in quenched Fe-16%Al versus denser tangles/cell formation after furnace cooling) is a prerequisite for deformation twinning in bcc crystals, so twinning appears the more readily the higher the Al content and the lower the temperature.
microstructure: After 14 days at 320 °C the crystal remains a single-phase bcc Fe-Al solid solution monocrystal, i.e. free of grain boundaries. In addition to the matrix, rare globular inclusions with diameters up to 30 µm are present and were identified as AlN by EDX analysis. Critically, no carbides were detected in this crystal after the 320 °C/14 d treatment. This contrasts with the polycrystals, where fine thin plate-like or rod-like precipitates believed to be carbides form on grain boundaries after slow furnace cooling from 1100 °C or prolonged annealing (14 days at 320 °C), their amount decreasing with lower C content; and with the Fe-17%Al monocrystal containing 70 ppm C, in which carbides appeared after 14 days at 320 °C only when the anneal was combined with concurrent 100 MPa loading, with much less carbide forming without loading. Without any heat treatment no carbides were found in any of the monocrystals.
processing: Step 1 — crystal growth: monocrystals up to 10 cm in length were grown by the Bridgman method at a pulling rate of 10–15 mm/h, the crystal growth with subsequent cooling taking about 12 h in total. The crystal was etched with ammonium persulfate ((NH4)2S2O8) and oriented using a laser light-figure method; its composition was verified by ICP. Step 2 — annealing: the Fe-16%Al monocrystal with 45 ppm C was heat-treated for 14 days at 320 °C. Following the experimental protocol of the study, this heat treatment was carried out with the specimen enclosed in an evacuated (10^-6 bar) SiO2 capsule; no Si uptake from the capsule was detectable under the chosen conditions (short anneals up to 300 °C were instead done in 99.99% pure argon). The 320 °C/14 d condition lies in the temperature window (below 600 °C) used in this work to vary the state of short-range order.
properties: No mechanical property value can be attributed specifically to this 320 °C/14 d condition. The (111)-oriented Fe-16%Al monocrystal was characterised by microhardness (universal hardness HU, Fischerscope H100, maximum load 1 N, averages of more than 40 measurements) and by room-temperature compressive stress-strain testing (10^-4 s^-1) as a function of prior heat treatment, but the hardness plot lists the conditions 300 °C/14 d (the lowest point, near 1875 N/mm²), 300 °C/6 h, 300 °C/3 d and 320 °C/233 d — not 320 °C/14 d — so no HU or yield-stress value is reported for this sample. Across all conditions the heat treatment shifts HU by only about 5–10% around ≈2000 N/mm², with the largest (still small) hardening produced by quenching from 1100 °C and the flow stress of the monocrystals changing only modestly (quenching plus 300 °C/14 d annealing giving the highest compressive curve). Characterisation methods applied to this material were metallographic inspection by optical microscopy after etching in an alcoholic 10% nitric acid solution (to reveal grain boundaries and precipitates/carbides) and qualitative precipitate/inclusion analysis by EDX in the SEM.
summary: This is a (111)-oriented Fe-16 at.% Al monocrystal (real composition 16.0 at.% Al, 8.4 wt.-%) containing 45 wt.ppm C, grown by the Bridgman method and subsequently annealed for 14 days at 320 °C in an evacuated SiO2 capsule. It is one of the binary Fe-Al monocrystals used in a study of the low-temperature deformation behaviour of iron-rich Fe-Al alloys, in which the effects of quenched-in excess vacancies and of short-range ordering on strength and ductility were separated by carefully controlling heat treatment and keeping carbon below 100 wt.ppm. The central, sample-specific result is that no carbides were detected in this crystal after the 320 °C/14 d treatment, in contrast to the carbide precipitation seen in polycrystals and in the Fe-17%Al monocrystal under concurrent loading.
unmapped: The Fe-16%Al monocrystal is (111)-oriented as used for the hardness study and [112]-oriented in the compressive stress-strain study; both the hardness (Fig. 1) and the compressive stress-strain (Fig. 2) datasets cover the same Fe-16% monocrystal material as a function of prior heat treatment, but neither reports a value for the 320 °C/14 d condition specifically (the nearest hardness conditions are 300 °C/14 d and 320 °C/233 d).

Across the study, hot-work/compression specimens measured 5 × 5 × 10 mm³, yield stress was taken as the 0.2% proof stress in compression (strains >=5%) at 10^-4 and 10^-2 s^-1, and the tensile specimens were prepared to DIN 50125; these test conditions apply to the alloy family rather than being a measured result of this particular 320 °C/14 d sample.
